sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage: This original retelling draws on the traditional myth. Arachne was a talented weaver who took great pride in her work. When people praised her skill, she insisted that no teacher or goddess deserved any credit. Athena, associated with wisdom and crafts, approached in disguise and advised her to speak with humility. Arachne dismissed the advice and demanded a contest. The two wove remarkable pictures, but their conflict involved more than technical skill: Arachne’s attitude challenged the goddess’s authority. In the traditional ending, Athena transformed Arachne into a spider, forever connected with weaving. Readers can admire Arachne’s ability while questioning her boastfulness and the severity of the punishment. The story invites discussion of pride, power, artistic skill, and the consequences of refusing advice. A theme is a reasoned interpretation, not simply the name of a topic.

sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage: In this original historical fiction, an apprentice watched an experienced builder inspect a Roman-style stone bridge. The apprentice wanted to remove the wooden supports as soon as the final stone was placed. "A finished appearance is not enough," the builder warned. He checked the arch and explained how its stones pressed against one another and transferred forces toward the supports. The apprentice grew impatient, but a cracked stone changed her mind. Together they replaced it and repeated the inspection. Later, the apprentice wrote that the delay had been the most important part of the work. The scene does not establish facts about a particular ancient builder; it uses an imagined conversation to explore patience and responsibility. Readers should distinguish the fictional characters from historical claims, such as the Romans’ use of arches in engineering.

sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage: Fictional classroom sources: Source A, "Weather Log," by a student team, dated March 8, records local temperature, wind direction, and pressure at noon for five days. Source B, an unsigned advertisement dated March 8, says that one device "always predicts weather perfectly" but gives no measurements. A research group prefers Source A for describing what was actually observed. It still checks the team’s instruments and method, because named authors and a date do not guarantee accuracy. The group writes a cautious forecast, separating data from inference. Its notes include each source’s title, creator, date, and the particular information used. In its final explanation, it paraphrases the data instead of copying a paragraph and identifies its source. Readers can judge the explanation more easily because the evidence and its limits are visible.

sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage: A community group argues that a school should plant trees near its outdoor learning area. Its claim is narrower than "trees solve every problem": a carefully chosen location may provide shade and support habitat. The group presents a fictional class data table comparing temperatures at a sunny spot and a shaded spot. It also acknowledges counterarguments: planting and watering cost money, and roots or branches may interfere with structures. Its proposal recommends consulting knowledgeable staff, selecting a suitable location, and comparing costs before planting. An effective response to a counterargument does not mock the people who raise it. Instead, it explains how the plan addresses a reasonable concern or why the evidence supports a different choice. The final paragraph asks the school to try a manageable plan and report the results.
